name: Act of March 2, 1889 dividing the Great Sioux Reservation (Sioux Agreement of 1889)
nations: Lakota, Dakota and Nakota (Oceti Sakowin) of the Great Sioux Reservation
promises: The Act, which the Indian Claims Commission records was accepted and agreed to by the different bands of the Sioux Nation, set apart separate reservations for groups of the nation out of the Great Reservation established by the 1868 treaty.
Section 5 described the Lower Brule reservation, its south line running along the forty-fourth degree of latitude.
Section 21 restored the rest of the Great Reservation to the public domain, to be disposed of for the benefit of the Sioux Nation and sold to settlers at prices the Act specified.

breaches.what: The Commission found that the 1890 government survey placed the Lower Brule south line 5,164 feet north of the true forty-fourth parallel, excluding 25,968.24 acres of the reservation the 1889 Act set apart. The United States treated that land as ceded and disposed of it from 1892 to 1911. Following the Court of Claims (125 C. Cls. 439), the Commission held the Lower Brule entitled to recover the land's value.

breaches.what: The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe says Congress further reduced the Great Sioux Reservation by the Act of March 2, 1889, opening the reservation to settlement by non-Indians and creating the checkerboarded land ownership that still drives jurisdiction disputes, while the Tribe holds its 1851 and 1868 treaty rights to be fully in force.

landTaken: 25,968.24 acres of the Lower Brule reservation were wrongly excluded by the 1890 survey (Docket 78, 1956).
compensation: For the Lower Brule survey strip: entitled to $18,818.11 plus interest ($71,747.63 in all), wholly offset by land purchases, so nothing was paid (Docket 78 Final Order, 1961).
today: The Lower Brule finding covers only the survey strip. The Black Hills taking of 1877 that preceded this Act is recorded under kappler-1006 and cession-1876-09-26-arapaho-northern-cheyenne-sioux. The Sioux sued under a 1920 jurisdictional act for the price the 1889 Act set for the ceded land: the Court of Claims held the United States accountable for $5,307,655.87, the proceeds of 9,261,592.62 acres, and rejected a claim to a further 271,482.57-acre strip west of the 103rd meridian as ceded in 1877 (97 Ct. Cl. 391, 1942). Its 1946 accounting found that fund used up by charges the Act allowed and dismissed the petition (105 Ct. Cl. 658). Neither is a finding against the United States, and no Indian Claims Commission finding on the 1889 price was found.

nationVoice.nation: Lower Brule Sioux Tribe (Kul Wicasa Oyate)
nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the United States, finding the Great Sioux Reservation the Lakota had agreed to intolerable, broke it up by the 1889 Act, splitting the Sicangu in two and moving the Lower Brule reservation north, and then took more of it in 1899 and 1906.

The Tribe says Congress greatly reduced the Great Sioux Reservation by the Act of March 2, 1889, dividing it into separate reservations and opening its land to non-Indian settlement, which left Standing Rock checkerboarded, and it holds that its 1851 and 1868 treaty rights remain as binding as the day they were made.

The Tribe says the Great Sioux Reservation created by the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty was later reduced to five reservations, from which Pine Ridge was established in 1889, and that the loss of land including the Black Hills remains a point of contention.

The Cheyenne River Sioux history the Tribe publishes says the Sioux Agreement Act of 1889 set the reservation's boundary lines, and that as reservation land was ceded the agency town had to move because it now lay outside the new boundaries.

openQuestions: Audit 2026-11-08: resolved. The Commission's 1961 opinion (9 Ind. Cl. Comm. 535, item 457) states the 1956 award as $19,476.18 and deducts $658.07 already credited to the Lower Brule by the Court of Claims, leaving $18,818.11, the figure in the final order.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): 105 Ct. Cl. 725 (1946) loaded from the Caselaw Access Project. Its rulings that rations and agency costs were illegally charged to reservation trust funds rest on the 1877 agreement and the 1895 to 1910 sale Acts, not on this cession, and the recoveries were wholly offset; it also declined jurisdiction over a Lower Brule claim to 34,664.62 acres excluded by the 1890 survey. Not added as a breach here.

Audit 2026-11-08 (round 14): the 1889 Act's price was litigated in Court of Claims case C-531 (11): 97 Ct. Cl. 391 (1942) and 105 Ct. Cl. 658 (1946), both against the Sioux; the judgment was re-entered in 1948 and certiorari denied in 1949 (cited in ICC Docket 119, 34 Ind. Cl. Comm. 230). ICC Docket 74 concerns the 1851 lands and 74-B the Black Hills; Dockets 114 to 119 are post-1925 accountings. None was found to hold the 1889 price unconscionable.
The Act's text was read only through the Commission's quotations; the Statutes at Large page (25 Stat. 888) was not opened.
No tribal history page about the 1889 Act loaded (the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe site blocked automated reading).
Ration cuts after 1889 and the reservation diminishment cases of the 1900s are not recorded here.

The 1956 Docket 78 opinion's figure for the total acreage ceded is unreadable in the scan; the Court of Claims gives 9,261,592.62 acres as the area the parties agreed passed under the cession (97 Ct. Cl. 391).

plain.promised: Separate reservations for groups of the Sioux Nation out of the Great Sioux Reservation, with the rest sold to settlers for the benefit of the Sioux Nation. The Lower Brule line was to run along the forty-fourth parallel.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1956 that an 1890 survey wrongly left 25,968.24 acres outside the Lower Brule reservation, and the United States disposed of them. Lower Brule and Standing Rock say the Act broke up the Great Sioux Reservation.
plain.today: The Lower Brule were owed $71,747.63 with interest, but the whole sum was offset against land the United States had bought for the tribe, so nothing was paid.
